tldr: Three US agencies named six Chinese AI firms for industrial-scale copying of American models, and told US labs to quietly serve them degraded answers.
US forces destroyed five Iranian oil tankers; Iran fired about 20 missiles at a US-used base in Jordan and struck 10 ships near Hormuz.
Brent crude passed $100 for the first time since July and markets flipped to betting the Fed hikes rates on September 16.
HHS awarded $383.4 million to the 988 crisis line and behavioral health programs, with $252 million for suicide prevention and mobile crisis teams.
Twelve governments including the UK, France and Canada banned trade with Israeli West Bank settlements; Israel closed Britain's Jerusalem consulate.
Mistral raised 3 billion euros at a 21 billion euro valuation, the largest equity round in European tech history, led by Samsung.
The US will bar most Canadian alcohol, motorcycles and some dairy from September 29 after Canada's $20 billion counter-tariffs took effect.
Cognition raised $2 billion at a $48 billion valuation, nearly doubling in four months on roughly $900 million of run-rate revenue.
Google patched the seventh Chrome zero-day already exploited in attacks this year, the second in a single week.
Trump promised every adult citizen $5,000 if Republicans hold Congress, a pledge the AP priced above $1 trillion and which Congress would have to pass.

items.headline: US agencies name six Chinese AI firms and advise American labs to serve them worse answers
items.body: The NSA, CISA and FBI issued joint advisory AA26-251A on September 8, accusing DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, Alibaba, MiniMax, StepFun and Z.AI of running "aggressive, malicious, and targeted" distillation campaigns against US frontier models since late 2024, extracting billions of tokens across millions of API exchanges with versions of Claude, GPT, Gemini and Grok. The agencies say the firms used fraudulent accounts, bulk premium subscriptions and proxy "transfer stations" to evade detection, and that DeepSeek's widely quoted $5.6 million training cost excludes data obtained this way. Rather than blocking suspect accounts, the advisory recommends providers answer them with silently downgraded models and vary the degradation so it cannot be measured.
items.plain: Distillation means using one AI's answers as training material for another. Send a leading model millions of questions, keep the answers, train your own cheaper model on them, and you inherit much of its skill without paying to build it. The agencies say six Chinese companies did this at industrial scale behind fake accounts and rented internet routes. The strange part is the advice: do not ban the accounts, just quietly give them worse answers, because a ban tells the copier exactly when it was caught.
items.why: An official US recommendation that AI providers secretly degrade output turns model access into a counterintelligence instrument, and any customer wrongly flagged would not be told their answers got worse.

items.headline: US sinks five Iranian tankers; Iran fires about 20 missiles at a US base in Jordan
items.body: CENTCOM said it destroyed five Iranian crude tankers on Tuesday - the Kaviz, Charminar, Horizon 1 and Riesco in the Gulf of Oman, and the Derya near Kharg Island - after the Revolutionary Guard fired ballistic missiles at a US warship twice in two days. Crews were ordered to abandon ship before the strikes and no US personnel were hurt. Iran retaliated Wednesday with roughly 20 ballistic missiles at a US-used base near Al-Azraq, Jordan; Jordan said its defenses intercepted 18, with two landing in unpopulated areas and no casualties. The Guard also said it attacked 10 ships near the Strait of Hormuz, including two US vessels and eight tankers. The war is in its sixth month, with Hormuz closed by Tehran and Iranian ports under US naval blockade.
items.plain: The Strait of Hormuz is a narrow sea passage that about a fifth of the world's oil normally travels through. Iran sits along it and has been firing at American warships; the US answers by sinking the tankers Iran uses to sell oil, which is how Iran earns money. So both sides are attacking each other's economy rather than each other's territory. Jordan matters because it hosts American forces, which lets Iran hit the US without hitting the United States itself.
items.why: Both sides are now aiming at shipping instead of land targets, which keeps casualties low and pushes the cost of the war onto everyone who buys oil.

items.headline: Brent crude passes $100 and markets flip to betting on a Fed rate hike
items.body: Brent crude reached $100.95 on Wednesday, its highest since July and up roughly 43% in nine weeks, after the US strikes on Iranian tankers. Futures markets moved to price a 52.5% chance the Federal Reserve raises rates by 25 basis points at its September 16 meeting, having priced no change as the dominant outcome a month earlier; other trackers put the odds nearer 68%, so the market is not settled. Euro-area inflation hit 3.3% in August on a 14.3% annual jump in energy prices, and all 65 economists in a Reuters poll expect the ECB to lift its deposit rate to 2.50% in a decision due at 12:15 GMT today.
items.plain: Central banks raise interest rates to cool inflation by making borrowing expensive. They usually look past an oil spike, because rate policy cannot fix a war. What changed is duration: the conflict is six months old, so traders now expect the higher price to stick and feed into anything shipped, heated or made. That is why the bet flipped from a cut or a hold to a possible increase. The two probability figures disagree, which is itself a sign the call is genuinely close.
items.why: A rate rise driven by a war premium tightens credit for households and firms that had nothing to do with the shock, and commits the Fed to treating the oil spike as lasting rather than temporary.

items.headline: HHS awards $383.4 million to the 988 crisis line and behavioral health programs
items.body: HHS, through the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration, announced on September 8 - designated 988 Day - that it had awarded $383.4 million in grants for behavioral health treatment, prevention and crisis response. Of that, $252 million goes to the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, suicide prevention and mobile crisis services, including $205.8 million in state and territory capacity-building agreements and $19.9 million for tribal 988 response. Another $81.4 million goes to substance use treatment and prevention and $50 million to mental health services, with $14.3 million for the National Child Traumatic Stress Initiative and $13.4 million for rural emergency medical services training.
items.plain: 988 is the three-digit number Americans call or text in a mental health crisis. It is not one call center: it is a network of state, tribal and local centers that actually answer, plus mobile teams that drive out instead of police being sent. Those centers run on federal grants that expire and must be renewed, so an award like this decides how many people are staffed to pick up next year. Most of this money is that staffing, not new programs.
items.why: The money funds the answering capacity behind the number, which is the part that fails first when call volume grows faster than the grants that pay for it.

items.headline: Twelve countries ban trade with Israeli West Bank settlements; Israel shuts the UK consulate
items.body: The UK, France and Canada announced on September 8 that they will ban imports of goods produced in Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank and East Jerusalem, part of a coordinated action by 12 governments that also includes Denmark, Spain, Finland, Ireland, Iceland, Norway, Poland, Portugal and Sweden. The bans cover settlement goods only, not goods from Israel itself; the UK went further with restrictions on services and fresh sanctions. Israel responded by announcing it would close Britain's consulate in East Jerusalem, which serves Palestinians. Three of the twelve governments are G7 members.
items.plain: Settlements are Israeli communities built on land Israel captured in 1967, which most governments treat as illegally occupied. Until now, objecting to them was mostly statements. This attaches a customs consequence: a crate of dates or a bottle of wine from a settlement is barred, while the identical product from inside Israel is not. That distinction is the entire design - it targets the settlements rather than the country, which is also why it is harder for Israel to dismiss as a boycott of Israel.
items.why: Separating settlement goods from Israeli goods at the border builds the customs machinery a far broader boycott would need, which is why Israel treated a narrow trade rule as a diplomatic rupture.

items.headline: Mistral raises 3 billion euros at a 21 billion euro valuation in Europe's largest equity round
items.body: Mistral said on September 8 it had raised 3 billion euros in a Series D at a post-money valuation above 21 billion euros, which the company called the largest equity fundraising ever completed by a European technology firm. Samsung Electronics led the round, with co-leads Scaleup Europe Fund, managed by EQT, and existing investor PSG Equity; Advent, funds managed by BlackRock and the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg joined as new investors. Mistral's previous round, a 1.7 billion euro Series C led by ASML in September 2025, valued it at 11.7 billion euros, so the valuation nearly doubled in a year. The company said the money goes to compute for training and to international expansion.
items.plain: Mistral is a French company that builds AI models and publishes many of their weights openly, which lets a government or a bank run the model on its own computers instead of sending data to an American provider. That pitch is called sovereign AI, and it is what a European state buys when it wants the capability without the dependency. Worth noticing: a champion of European technological independence just took its largest cheque from a South Korean chipmaker.
items.why: European governments and enterprises are now paying a premium for AI they can host themselves, a market that barely existed two years ago and that US providers cannot serve on the same terms.

items.headline: US will block most Canadian alcohol, motorcycles and some dairy from September 29
items.body: The White House published import bans covering most Canadian alcoholic beverages, motorcycles and some dairy products, effective September 29, and added further products to a list subject to 50% tariffs. The move followed Canada's own retaliatory tariffs, roughly $20 billion of US goods, which took effect after midnight on Tuesday. Prime Minister Mark Carney said Canada was not seeking to escalate but could not let American goods enter tariff-free while Canadian companies face US tariffs. Outright import bans, rather than tariffs, are an unusual instrument between two countries whose economies are this closely joined.
items.plain: A tariff is a tax that makes a foreign product more expensive; a ban means it cannot be sold at any price. Washington had been using tariffs on Canada, Canada answered with tariffs on about $20 billion of American goods, and Washington has now escalated to bans on named categories. Whisky, motorcycles and cheese are chosen for politics rather than economics: they come from places whose politicians and voters will make the loudest noise.
items.why: Moving from tariffs to bans removes the price mechanism entirely, so affected Canadian producers lose the US market outright rather than losing margin on it.

items.headline: Cognition raises $2 billion at a $48 billion valuation as coding-agent revenue climbs
items.body: Cognition, which makes the software-engineering agent Devin, raised $2 billion at a $48 billion valuation in a round led by Andreessen Horowitz with Accel, Founders Fund, General Catalyst and Avenir. The company was valued at $26 billion in May, when run-rate revenue was $492 million; that figure is now close to $900 million, and Cognition is projected to reach $4 billion to $5 billion annualized by the end of 2026. It was founded in 2024 by chief executive Scott Wu. The new valuation implies roughly 53 times current run-rate revenue.
items.plain: Devin is sold as an agent rather than an assistant: you describe the task and it plans the work, writes and tests the code, fixes what breaks and deploys it, inside a sandbox where it cannot touch anything else. Investors are paying about 53 times current annual revenue, which only makes sense if that revenue keeps roughly doubling. The signal to catch is that a challenger to bigger coding tools can still raise at this size, meaning investors do not expect one winner.
items.why: Two AI companies raised $5 billion between them on the same day at prices set by revenue growth rather than research promise, a different kind of bet than the field was making a year ago.

items.headline: Google patches the seventh Chrome zero-day already used in attacks this year
items.body: Google's September 8 Chrome stable release fixed CVE-2026-87491, an out-of-bounds write in V8, the engine that runs JavaScript and WebAssembly inside the browser, which can be triggered by a malicious web page. It is the seventh Chrome zero-day exploited in the wild that Google has patched in 2026, and the second in a single week. Google confirmed an exploit exists but has not said who is using it, who was targeted, or how it is delivered. The fix ships in Chrome 153.0.8010.36 and .37 for Windows and macOS and .36 for Linux; Chrome 153 carried 230 security fixes in total, five rated critical. CISA has told federal agencies to patch by September 23.
items.plain: A zero-day is a flaw attackers are already using before a fix exists, so there is no safe version to be on until the update ships. This one sits in the part of Chrome that runs code from web pages, so visiting the wrong page is enough - no download, no click. An out-of-bounds write means the code writes data past the end of the memory reserved for it, overwriting things it should not, which is how an attacker gets their own instructions to run. Restarting the browser is what applies the patch.
items.why: Seven exploited browser flaws in nine months, two of them in one week, suggests exploit buyers are finding V8 bugs faster than Google's hardening is closing that class of bug off.

items.headline: Trump pledges $5,000 to every adult citizen if Republicans hold Congress
items.body: At the Republican midterm convention in Dallas on Wednesday, September 9, Trump said: "if the Republicans win the House of Representatives and the United States Senate, both of them ... because of our tremendous strength and success economically, I will issue a dividend to every adult citizen in the United States of America for $5,000," adding, "So if the Republicans win, you win with us and you get $5,000 dollars. It will be called the Trump dividend." The Associated Press put the cost above $1 trillion and noted it would require congressional approval, against a federal deficit AP described as nearly $1.8 trillion a year; Fortune, citing CBO, reported deficits reaching $2 trillion for 2026 and $1.05 trillion spent servicing the debt over 11 months, about $95 billion a month. In February 2025 Trump endorsed a similar $5,000 "DOGE dividend," saying "I love it. A 20% dividend, so to speak, for the money that we're saving." No such payment was ever authorized.
items.plain: A president cannot send out money on his own, because Congress writes spending laws. So this is a promise conditional on an election result, for a payment a different branch would have to approve. Hold on to the scale: $5,000 to every adult citizen costs more than $1 trillion, in a year the government is already borrowing something between $1.8 trillion and $2 trillion, depending on whose figure you use, and paying roughly $95 billion a month in interest on past borrowing. He made effectively the same offer in February 2025 and nobody was paid.
items.why: Making the payment contingent on the vote converts a fiscal proposal into a campaign incentive, without any of the appropriations work that would make it real.
